title: The One With The Tiny T Shirt

jokes.text: Gunther rehearsing asking Rachel out, adding 'as my lover' to completely normal invitations
jokes.setup: Gunther is clearly rehearsing how to ask Rachel out, starting with a movie invitation
jokes.punchline: He tacks on '...as my lover' to an otherwise normal movie invitation, immediately recognizes it's wrong, then does the same thing again with a dinner invitation
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully constructed cold open joke. The escalation of Gunther correcting himself and then immediately making the exact same mistake with the exact same creepy phrase is perfect comedic structure. 'As my lover' is specific, bizarre, and completely in character for Gunther's delusional romantic fixation. The repetition is the joke — he learns nothing. High character integration because only Gunther's particular brand of hopeless, grandiose obsession makes this work.

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: Rachel, I was wondering if you'd like to go out with me... as my lover.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Um, what?

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: I mean, as my date. As my lover... I mean, eventually as my lover, but first as my date.

jokes.text: Mark tells Rachel he has a crush on her; long pause; then a crash from the kitchen
jokes.setup: Mark delivers a heartfelt confession of his feelings for Rachel while Gunther is presumably within earshot behind the counter
jokes.punchline: A dramatic crash from the kitchen (Gunther dropping a cup, devastated by what he's overheard) punctuates the emotional moment with a physical comedy beat
jokes.explanation: Exceptional structural comedy. The crash and then Gunther's sheepish 'I dropped a cup' after a beat of silence is a masterclass in visual/audio comedy staging. The joke works on multiple layers: it pays off the cold open's Gunther setup, it undercuts the romantic tension of Mark's confession, and Gunther's understated explanation ('I dropped a cup') is perfect deadpan. The timing between the crash and the explanation is where the real laugh lives. High rewatch value because viewers re-appreciate the setup knowing Gunther was listening.

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: That was too bold. I shouldn't have quoted that movie line.

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: But I still ended it the same way... as my lover.

jokes.text: GUNTHER: 'I dropped a cup.'
jokes.setup: A loud crash has come from the kitchen after Gunther overheard Mark confessing feelings for Rachel
jokes.punchline: Gunther's tiny, flat explanation — 'I dropped a cup' — as though nothing emotionally devastating just happened to him
jokes.explanation: Four words that do enormous comedic and emotional work. The deadpan delivery of this explanation after a catastrophic emotional moment is the punchline to joke #2's setup. It scores slightly higher on economy than the crash itself because the LINE is the distilled joke. Gunther's pathetic stoicism is both funny and oddly touching. This type of two-part physical/verbal payoff is professional-grade sitcom writing.

jokes.text: Joey's date explaining voice recognition: 'You could be like, Wash my car. Clean my room.' — 'It's not gonna be able to do any of those things, but it'll understand what you're saying.'
jokes.setup: Joey is on a date with a woman explaining the exciting future of voice recognition technology on computers
jokes.punchline: The technology's only actual capability is understanding your words — not performing any of the tasks you'd logically want it to do
jokes.explanation: A decent observational joke about tech hype that holds up surprisingly well. The structure is solid — raise the promise, then immediately deflate it. Low character integration because this joke could come from almost any character; it's not specifically Joey. The humor is in the gap between what people want technology to do and what it actually does. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: I dropped a cup.

jokes.text: Chandler and Joey are in Monica's apartment; Monica says 'I gave you a key for emergencies'; Joey says 'We were out of Doritos.'
jokes.setup: Monica confronts Chandler and Joey for being in her apartment uninvited, pointing out she gave them a key for emergencies
jokes.punchline: Joey casually reveals the 'emergency' was being out of Doritos, treating a snack shortage as a genuine crisis
jokes.explanation: Clean, well-executed character joke. 'We were out of Doritos' is perfectly Joey — his relationship with food being treated with the same gravity as any genuine emergency is consistent characterization. The economy is strong; the punchline lands quickly. Not groundbreaking but professionally executed.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: The technology will understand your commands perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: But it can't actually do anything useful with them.

jokes.text: 'Mr. Millionaire. New, from Snooty Playthings. Third wife sold separately.'
jokes.setup: Joey asks how Monica's date with the wealthy Pete went, calling him 'Mr. Millionaire'
jokes.punchline: Chandler riffs on 'Mr. Millionaire' as if it's a toy from a luxury brand called 'Snooty Playthings,' complete with the dark kicker that the 'third wife' is sold separately
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Chandler takes Joey's throwaway phrase and instantly constructs an entire satirical product with a brand name, a category, and a dark accessory joke. 'Snooty Playthings' is an inspired brand name. 'Third wife sold separately' implies a history of failed marriages and escalating wealth simultaneously — two jokes in one. This is exactly the kind of quick-riff comedy Chandler is built for, and the joke is layered enough to reward the audience. Strong quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, we're out of chips!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: This is definitely an emergency.

jokes.text: 'He has everything. Plus, he actually has everything.'
jokes.setup: Monica is listing Pete's virtues as a boyfriend
jokes.punchline: She uses 'he has everything' figuratively, then immediately clarifies she means it literally — he is actually, materially rich
jokes.explanation: A compact, well-structured wordplay joke built on the dual meaning of 'has everything.' The repetition with a pivot from figurative to literal is clean and earns its laugh. Good economy. Slightly generic but elevated by the self-aware delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey kids! Tired of playing with your boring old toys? Well, now there's Mr. Millionaire! Just wind him up and watch as he buys his way out of every problem! And when he gets tired of you, he can afford to leave you behind! Mr. Millionaire comes with a tiny checkbook and a complete inability to form meaningful relationships. Warning: May cause low self-esteem and trust issues. Mr. Millionaire—because money can't buy you love, but it can sure try!

jokes.text: Life-sized Imperial Stormtroopers from Sharper Image — and there are two of them
jokes.setup: Monica is listing Pete's impressive material possessions as evidence he 'actually has everything'
jokes.punchline: She mentions life-sized Imperial Stormtroopers from Sharper Image — and when Ross asks how many, she says 'Two,' implying a full guard detail
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Sharper Image' grounds an absurd visual detail in plausible millionaire excess. The follow-up of 'Two' when asked 'How many?' is the real punchline — of course he has two. Good use of escalation via a single word answer.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He has everything. He has a bidet. Not just a bidet—he has *bidets*. Plural.

jokes.text: Chandler pretending to be a Stormtrooper: 'Oh, Mommy. Oh, Daddy. I am a big old baddy.'
jokes.setup: Ross asks if he and Joey can put on the life-sized Stormtrooper suits and fight
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately slips into character as a Stormtrooper with a hilariously un-intimidating, childlike rhyme
jokes.explanation: The contrast between the iconic menace of a Stormtrooper and Chandler's silly nursery-rhyme improvisation is the joke. 'Oh, Mommy. Oh, Daddy. I am a big old baddy' is charmingly bad in a way that reflects Chandler's particular brand of ironic goofiness. Gets a big physical comedy laugh from the audience. Solid moment.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. These are worth how much? Thousands of dollars? Each?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God. I have to have them. I'm gonna open that box right now and play with them.

jokes.text: Ross entering the apartment dancing, prompting the Gloria Estefan joke
jokes.setup: Ross enters the apartment dancing, apparently in a good mood
jokes.punchline: Chandler remarks: 'Either that or Gloria Estefan was right. Eventually, the rhythm is going to get you.'
jokes.explanation: A decent pop-culture reference joke that works because of the specificity of 'Gloria Estefan' and the earnest application of 'Rhythm Is Gonna Get You' to Ross's dancing. Competent Chandler riff but not among the episode's best.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I am a Stormtrooper! Resistance is futile! You will bow before my imperial power!

jokes.text: Kate to Joey: 'Are you one of the retarded cousins?'
jokes.setup: Joey approaches Kate at rehearsal and asks if she's playing Adrianne; Kate has apparently sized him up quickly
jokes.punchline: Kate fires back asking if he's playing one of the 'retarded cousins' in the play — a sharp, dismissive put-down implying he looks like he belongs in that role
jokes.explanation: Establishes Kate's sharp, dismissive personality and sets up the antagonistic dynamic with Joey. The insult is quick and specific to the play's context, which gives it more craft than a generic put-down. The word choice is dated by modern standards. Functional character-establishing humor.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you got the part!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? No, no, no.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, you're dancing.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, the rhythm is gonna get me.

jokes.text: Joey describing Jennifer Banberry: 'She's so brilliantly incisive when it comes to deconstructing the psyche of the middle class.' / 'Oh, forget about it. She rocks.'
jokes.setup: Kate gushes about the playwright using sophisticated critical vocabulary
jokes.punchline: Joey starts to match her intellectual register, then collapses into 'Oh, forget about it. She rocks.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. The setup is Joey clearly repeating something he heard or read (he can recite the phrase but has no idea what it means), and the punchline collapses all that pretension into 'She rocks.' The contrast between the highbrow language and the slang is perfectly timed and deeply Joey. High character integration — this only works because of who Joey is.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So you're playing Adrianne?

dialogue.speaker: Kate
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's great! I'm playing Bryce.

dialogue.speaker: Kate
dialogue.line: Oh. So you're the guy I sleep with in the movie?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah!

dialogue.speaker: Kate
dialogue.line: Oh. I thought you'd be taller.

jokes.text: Kate: 'Where do I know you from?' / Joey: 'Dr. Drake Ramoray? Days of our Lives? Voted most datable neurosurgeon by Teen Beat?'
jokes.setup: Kate is trying to place Joey's face; Joey assumes she recognizes him from his soap opera fame
jokes.punchline: Joey lists his credentials with increasing self-importance, ending with 'voted most datable neurosurgeon by Teen Beat' — a meaningless honor that he treats as a major accolade
jokes.explanation: The escalating specificity of Joey's credentials is perfectly calibrated — each item is more absurd than the last. 'Voted most datable neurosurgeon by Teen Beat' is the ideal punchline because it combines the specific silliness of his soap character with the meaninglessness of being recognized by a teen magazine. High character integration: this is completely and only Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Kate
dialogue.line: The playwright's utilization of postmodern deconstructionist methodology creates a liminal space where the audience confronts the inherent contradictions of contemporary existence.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: She rocks.

jokes.text: Kate: 'No, that's not it. So you're a soap actor. Well, this must be exciting for you, being in a real play.'
jokes.setup: Joey has just listed his soap opera credentials proudly; Kate didn't recognize him from any of that
jokes.punchline: Kate dismisses his entire career with condescension, implying his soap work isn't 'real' acting — a theatrical snob's put-down delivered smoothly
jokes.explanation: Good character-establishing joke for Kate — her theatrical snobbery is immediately clear. The condescension is well-delivered and sets up the Joey-Kate antagonism that will fuel the rest of the episode. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Kate
dialogue.line: Do I know you from somewhere?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, I'm an actor. You might've seen me on TV.

dialogue.speaker: Kate
dialogue.line: Hmm, I don't think so.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh! I was on a World War I documentary. I played a guy who got shot. It was really moving.

dialogue.speaker: Kate
dialogue.line: I don't watch much TV.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, I also did a mattress commercial where I jumped on a bed for eight hours. Or you could know me from my work as a smell-o-vision consultant, where I help people identify odors.

dialogue.speaker: Kate
dialogue.line: I really don't think—

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait! Do you hang out at the park? Because I once taught a pigeon to say 'Hello.' Maybe you heard that pigeon.

jokes.text: Kate: 'That infomercial.' / '...For the milk-carton-spout thing. You're the guy who doesn't know how to pour milk.'
jokes.setup: Joey insists he's a serious actor; Kate is trying to place where she knows him from
jokes.punchline: She remembers him from an infomercial where he plays someone too incompetent to pour milk from a carton
jokes.explanation: This is a strong joke because it perfectly undercuts Joey's 'serious actor' pretension at exactly the right moment. The specificity of 'the milk-carton-spout thing' and 'the guy who doesn't know how to pour milk' is inspired — it's a completely believable infomercial premise and a humiliating credit for a wannabe-serious actor. Sets up the next joke perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Kate
dialogue.line: Wait, weren't you on Days of Our Lives?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, I played Dr. Drake Ramoray for—

dialogue.speaker: Kate
dialogue.line: Oh right, that show. Well, it's nice you're doing something more... legitimate now.

jokes.text: Joey: 'See, I actually can pour milk. But I got you believing that I couldn't. Now, see, that's acting.' Kate: 'Right. At the end, you choked on a cookie.' Joey: 'Yeah, that was real.'
jokes.setup: Joey tries to spin his infomercial role as evidence of his acting skill — he was PRETENDING not to know how to pour milk
jokes.punchline: Kate points out he choked on a cookie at the end; Joey admits that was genuine, completely destroying his argument
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's standout joke. The structure is flawless: Joey's defense of himself as an actor (he was PRETENDING to be incompetent) is genuinely clever and earns a moment of grudging respect — then Kate destroys it with the cookie detail, and Joey's 'Yeah, that was real' is the perfect surrender. The callback to an established detail in the same scene, the escalation from setup to defense to total collapse, and Joey's complete lack of awareness all combine into something genuinely excellent. 'Yeah, that was real' is a top-tier sitcom punchline — short, devastating, character-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Kate
dialogue.line: Oh my God! I know where I know you from!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You do?

dialogue.speaker: Kate
dialogue.line: Yes! You were in that adult film... 'The Shining: The XXX Parody'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I... that was a very small role

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'Wow. So, okay, maybe that means you're not over Ross yet and you have issues with your father.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is explaining the guilt she felt when Mark asked her out, as if she'd be cheating on Ross
jokes.punchline: Phoebe immediately leaps to a pop-psychology conclusion that Rachel has 'issues with her father' — a non-sequitur armchair diagnosis
jokes.explanation: Classic Phoebe — she correctly identifies one thing (the Ross issue) and then confidently throws in a Freudian non-sequitur. The father reference comes out of nowhere and is immediately deflated when Rachel denies it, leading Phoebe to casually drop it. Good character integration for Phoebe's pseudo-wise, free-associating personality.

dialogue.speaker: Kate
dialogue.line: You were in an infomercial?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It was a very important commercial. I played the guy who had the problem.

dialogue.speaker: Kate
dialogue.line: The problem was what, exactly?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I had really bad joints. But then I discovered this great lubricant and my life changed.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'I don't have any issues with my father.' Phoebe: 'Okay, so it's probably just the Ross thing.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just suggested Rachel has issues with her father; Rachel denies it
jokes.punchline: Phoebe instantly abandons the father theory with complete equanimity, as if it was just a casual guess that didn't pan out
jokes.explanation: The follow-through on Phoebe's non-sequitur is almost funnier than the original. Her breezy 'Okay, so it's probably just the Ross thing' treats a major pop-psychology detour as a perfectly reasonable wrong answer she's happy to drop. Good economy and character-perfect Phoebe behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: The milk thing was acting. I was just doing a bit.

dialogue.speaker: Kate
dialogue.line: What about when you choked on the cookie?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That was real.

jokes.text: Joey complaining that Kate told everyone about the infomercial and now they ask him to open their drinks, laughing when he can't
jokes.setup: Joey reveals Kate has spread the news of his infomercial to the cast
jokes.punchline: The infomercial was about a milk-carton spout, so now people ask him to open their drinks — and laugh when he can't, implying he actually might not be able to despite his insistence that he can
jokes.explanation: A solid callback that extends the infomercial joke and adds a new layer: the humiliation has gone public, and Joey's protests of competence are further undermined by the implication that he actually can't open drinks either. Good running gag escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, it's not your father issues.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I don't have father issues!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Then it's the Ross thing.

jokes.text: Ross hoping Rachel called because 'the crazy fog has lifted and she realizes that life without me sucks'
jokes.setup: Chandler asks what Ross thinks Rachel wants when she called to see him
jokes.punchline: Ross delivers this delusional, self-centered fantasy with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Ross's delusional hope is perfectly in character for his relationship blindness at this point in the series. 'The crazy fog has lifted' is a nice phrase, implying Rachel is temporarily insane for not wanting to be with him. Good character work, not exceptional comedy writing.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Maybe she wants to get back together!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Or maybe she just wants to talk about us, you know, as friends.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Or—or maybe she realized she made a huge mistake and she's been miserable without me this whole time!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's probably it.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'It's possible. You are very lovable. I'd miss you if I broke up with you.'
jokes.setup: Ross is hoping Rachel wants to get back together; Chandler is trying to be supportive
jokes.punchline: Chandler's support takes the form of saying he'd personally miss Ross if THEY broke up — accidentally making it about himself in a sweetly absurd way
jokes.explanation: A characteristically Chandler moment — his attempt at supportive friendship awkwardly pivots to a hypothetical about himself and Ross that sounds vaguely romantic. The absurdity of 'if I broke up with you' is played completely straight, which makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You really think Rachel might want me back?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah man, I think she does. And you know what? Even if she doesn't, you're still a great guy. You're smart, you're funny, you're... you're really attractive.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Thanks Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I mean it. If I were a woman, I would totally do you.

jokes.text: Ross: 'Well, be supportive like a guy.' Chandler [in deep voice]: 'If I broke up with you, I'd miss you.'
jokes.setup: Ross tells Chandler to be 'supportive like a guy' after Chandler's tender declaration
jokes.punchline: Chandler simply drops his voice an octave and says the exact same thing — implying masculine emotional expression is identical to feminine, just deeper
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback structure. Ross asks for masculine support; Chandler's commentary on male emotional performance is simply to pitch his voice lower and say the identical thing. The joke lands on two levels: it's funny as a bit, and it makes a sharp point about gendered emotional expression. Very economical — the entire joke is one repeated line with a vocal change.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey man, I'm here for you. You know, whatever you need, I got your back.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: We're bros. Bros help bros out. That's what it's all about.

jokes.text: Ross insisting the museum gift shop mug is a 'gift': 'I got it from the gift shop.'
jokes.setup: Rachel gives Ross back his things; he protests that one item was 'a gift'; she points out he got it free from the museum gift shop
jokes.punchline: Ross doubles down: 'It's still a gift. I got it from the gift shop.' — using the word 'gift' in the store name as literal evidence
jokes.explanation: Ross's stubborn circular logic — 'it's from the gift shop therefore it's a gift' — is a nice character moment. The wordplay isn't sophisticated but the petty logic is very Ross-specific and gets a laugh from the audience. Solid episode-specific character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, you can't just give me a mug you got for free from work and call it a gift.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Why not? I gave it to you. That makes it a gift.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, a gift is something you actually buy for someone.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I didn't have to give it to you. I chose to. That's what makes it a gift.

jokes.text: Ross demanding back the T-shirt Rachel sleeps in — 'And that T-shirt you sleep in? I'd like that back too.'
jokes.setup: Ross is reclaiming his possessions from Rachel's apartment in a fit of pique after the breakup
jokes.punchline: He demands back a shirt she wears to bed — knowing exactly what she sleeps in, which is simultaneously creepy, pathetically petty, and reveals how much he still cares
jokes.explanation: The specificity of Ross knowing what she sleeps in and demanding it back is simultaneously funny and a little devastating. It's a well-observed beat about how breakups make people petty and irrational in revealing ways. Good character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You're being so petty!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I am not petty!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yes, you are.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I am NOT petty!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You're being petty right now.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, maybe I AM a little petty, but I have a good reason! This shirt is TINY!

jokes.text: The 'petty, petty, petty... small, small' duet between Ross and Rachel
jokes.setup: Rachel calls Ross petty for wanting the T-shirt back; Ross and Rachel start trading the words 'petty' and 'small' in a petty argument about pettiness
jokes.punchline: They loop the words — 'petty, petty, petty... small, small... petty, petty, small' — in a perfect demonstration of the very pettiness being discussed
jokes.explanation: A meta-comedic moment where the form matches the content: they are being petty while arguing about pettiness. The escalating, overlapping word repetition is a strong physical/verbal comedy bit that builds naturally from the scene. It's cringe comedy that earns its laugh through structural cleverness rather than shock. The tag — Rachel saying 'You are so just doing this out of spite' while Ross denies it — caps it well.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, that shirt doesn't fit you.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It fits fine! It fits great!

jokes.text: Ross squeezing himself into Rachel's tiny T-shirt — the visual gag of it not fitting
jokes.setup: Ross insists he loves the shirt and wears it all the time; Rachel points out it hasn't fit since he was 15
jokes.punchline: Ross puts it on anyway (it's clearly a tiny, tight, ridiculous fit) and then calmly says 'Now, if you don't mind, I'm gonna take the rest of my stuff and relax in my favorite shirt'
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy payoff of the T-shirt subplot is excellent. Ross forces himself into a shirt that clearly doesn't fit and then maintains complete dignity — 'relax in my favorite shirt' — as if nothing is wrong. The commitment to the bit is what makes it land. The visual of Ross walking out in a tiny shirt is one of the episode's most memorable images. Strong rewatch value because you can see it coming but the execution still delivers.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What about Joey? Wait, that's a name... Joeyville? No... The State of Joey! No wait, New Joey!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh! Joey-homa!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: New... New Joey... New New Jersey!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Joeyfornia!

jokes.text: Ross insisting on keeping the tiny T-shirt, claiming 'I'm gonna wear this all the time. I love this shirt.'
jokes.setup: Rachel points out Ross hasn't worn the tiny T-shirt since he was 15 and it doesn't fit
jokes.punchline: Ross defiantly puts it on (clearly comically small on him) and insists he loves it and will wear it all the time
jokes.explanation: The visual of Ross in a tiny, ill-fitting T-shirt as an act of pure spite is the episode's title joke and it delivers well. The physical comedy of a grown man squeezed into a childhood shirt paired with his dignified exit ('You have a pleasant evening') is very funny. Strong visual gag with excellent character integration — only Ross does this kind of wounded, petty dignity.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Chicago isn't a state, Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, maybe I like to think outside the box, Chandler. Maybe Chicago should be a state!

jokes.text: Ross sweeps out saying 'You have a pleasant evening' while visibly crammed into a tiny T-shirt
jokes.setup: Ross has made a show of wearing the tiny T-shirt as a power move
jokes.punchline: He attempts a dignified exit with a formal farewell while looking completely ridiculous
jokes.explanation: The formal 'You have a pleasant evening' is perfectly calibrated — it's the register of someone who thinks they've won an argument, deployed while looking absurd. Ross's commitment to dignity while being undignified is a core character trait and this is a great expression of it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, he's our age?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, he's like 27 or something.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: And he's a millionaire?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Multi-millionaire.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: At 27?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Apparently.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What are we doing with our lives?

jokes.text: Joey: 'You should buy a state and name it after yourself. Like Pete Dakota.' Monica: 'Mississi-Pete.' Joey: 'Ooh, ooh, I got it: Pete Chicago.' Chandler: 'That's not a state, Joe.' Joey: 'Oh, and Mississi-Pete is?'
jokes.setup: The group is marveling at Pete's wealth; Joey suggests he buy a state and name it after himself
jokes.punchline: Joey proposes 'Pete Chicago,' is corrected that Chicago isn't a state, and defends himself by pointing out that 'Mississi-Pete' isn't a real state name either — which is technically true
jokes.explanation: The escalating geography game is a strong group comedy moment. 'Pete Dakota' → 'Mississi-Pete' → 'Pete Chicago' is a well-structured escalation. But the real gem is Joey's comeback: 'Oh, and Mississi-Pete is?' — he correctly identifies the logical inconsistency in being corrected for his suggestion when the previous suggestion was equally ridiculous. Joey's accidental logic is a signature comedic device for the character and this is a clean execution of it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I know we haven't really... touched much.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: But that's okay. I mean, we can work on that.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Pete, I care about you, but I don't think I'm in love with you.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'That's not a state, Joe.' Joey: 'Oh, and Mississi-Pete is?'
jokes.setup: Chandler corrects Joey for suggesting 'Pete Chicago' isn't a state
jokes.punchline: Joey points out that 'Mississi-Pete,' which Chandler didn't object to, is also not a real state name
jokes.explanation: Scoring this separately from the broader sequence because this specific exchange is the sharpest joke in the run. Joey's 'Oh, and Mississi-Pete is?' is genuinely clever — he's accidentally right, using flawless internal logic. It's a perfect Joey joke because it sounds dumb but is actually correct. The economy is exceptional: seven words that land a perfect punch. This is among the episode's best jokes alongside the cookie/milk bit.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, there's nothing wrong with you. You just have really bad taste in men.

jokes.text: Monica: 'Okay, I'm running out of places I can touch him.'
jokes.setup: Monica is dating Pete but feels no physical attraction; we've just watched her awkwardly send him off
jokes.punchline: She confesses she's literally running out of socially acceptable body parts to touch when saying goodbye, implying she's been avoiding any contact that might feel intimate
jokes.explanation: A nicely observed joke about the physical awkwardness of being with someone you like but aren't attracted to. The specificity of 'running out of places I can touch him' implies she's been systematically working through neutral body parts (shoulders, elbows, etc.) which is a funny visual. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! That was... that was really something.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I mean, for a stage kiss, that had some real heat to it.

jokes.text: Joey watching Kate and the director rehearse an intense emotional scene and commenting 'Tasty.'
jokes.setup: Kate is performing an emotionally intense, raw theatrical scene about a loveless marriage
jokes.punchline: Joey watches with what the director reads as deep emotional engagement — but Joey's summary of it is 'Tasty,' treating the intense drama like a good meal
jokes.explanation: 'Tasty' is a one-word punchline that perfectly captures Joey's inability to engage with emotional depth on an intellectual level — he processes it physically. The director misreads his animal appreciation as artistic sensitivity, which adds another layer. Very economic joke.

dialogue.speaker: Kate
dialogue.line: But what's the deeper motivation? Why are you attracted to this character?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, it says right here in the script that I am.

jokes.text: Director: 'I'm really starting to feel like you guys have a history. It's nice.'
jokes.setup: Joey has just responded to Kate's dramatic monologue with 'Tasty' (clearly eating)
jokes.punchline: The director interprets the awkward non-connection as chemistry — 'I'm really starting to feel like you guys have a history'
jokes.explanation: Good button on the previous joke. The director's complete misreading of the scene (seeing profound connection where there's only indifference and food) is a solid ironic beat. 'It's nice' is the perfect underplayed sign-off.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: The script says your character's a bitch.

dialogue.speaker: Kate
dialogue.line: It does not!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, it does now.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Well, I don't understand why Adrianne's attracted to Victor.' Director: 'Peel the onion. First of all, he's good-looking.' Joey: 'Yeah.' Kate: 'I think my character is gonna need a bit more of a reason than that.'
jokes.setup: Joey questions why his character's wife would be attracted to him; the director says 'he's good-looking'; Joey accepts this immediately
jokes.punchline: Kate sarcastically says her character needs 'a bit more of a reason than that' — implying good looks alone aren't sufficient dramatic motivation, while Joey has already accepted it as perfectly sufficient
jokes.explanation: A decent scene that uses the contrast between Joey's shallow acceptance ('yeah') and Kate's theatrical snobbery to generate humor. The director's 'Peel the onion' pomposity is also quietly funny. Not a standout moment but it moves the Joey-Kate dynamic forward with laughs.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Does my cowlick bug you?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, but you do.

jokes.text: Director: 'It says so in the script.' / Joey: 'You know, I don't know why my character likes you either. I mean, it says in the script that you're a bitch.' Kate: 'It doesn't say that.' Joey: 'It does in mine.'
jokes.setup: The director shuts down Kate's question about motivation by saying 'it says so in the script'; Joey then uses the same logic to insult Kate directly
jokes.punchline: When Kate denies the script says she's a bitch, Joey says 'It does in mine' — implying he's annotated his script with personal notes, or is simply lying with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best exchanges. Joey weaponizes the director's dismissive logic against Kate in a move that's simultaneously dense and perfectly targeted. 'It does in mine' is a brilliant punchline — it could mean he's written it in, or he's simply asserting a counter-reality with full confidence. The ambiguity makes it funnier. Very high character integration: this is exactly how Joey would fight back. Strong quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Did anyone see that?

jokes.text: Chandler's cowlick complaint: 'I can blow-dry it, I can put gel on it. It doesn't matter. I still wind up with this little cowlick-y thing on the middle part of my head. It's so annoying.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is complaining about a hair problem to Monica/Rachel in what appears to be a mundane conversation
jokes.punchline: 'Does it bug you?' — Monica/Rachel asks; Chandler: 'You bug me.'
jokes.explanation: A filler scene. The cowlick complaint itself is mundane, and 'You bug me' as a retort is a mild comeback. The humor is in Chandler's outsized irritation about a minor grooming issue, which is somewhat in character, but the joke doesn't land with much force. Below average for this episode.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey, you know what? I think you might have Peeping Tom syndrome.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's not a real condition.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, neither is my Chandler's syndrome, but I have that.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'You're gonna get peep-eye.'
jokes.setup: Ross has been staring through the peephole for three hours watching Rachel's apartment
jokes.punchline: Chandler warns him he'll get 'peep-eye' — a made-up condition riffing on 'pink eye,' implying extended peephole use has medical consequences
jokes.explanation: A compact, well-made wordplay joke. 'Peep-eye' is a natural portmanteau of 'peephole' and 'pink eye' that sounds just medically plausible enough to be funny. Chandler's delivery of this as a genuine health warning is perfectly dry. Good economy: two words do the whole job.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Three seconds? That's not a rebound, that's a world record! He went from 'we were on a break' to sleeping with someone faster than a bullet travels!

jokes.text: Chandler: 'You slept with somebody three hours after you thought you broke up. I mean, bullets have left guns slower.'
jokes.setup: Ross claims they 'just broke up' and Rachel shouldn't be moving on; Chandler pushes back on Ross's timeline
jokes.punchline: 'Bullets have left guns slower' — a sharp, specific simile for how fast Ross moved on
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Bullets have left guns slower' is a genuinely excellent simile — unexpected, precise, and funny. It's the kind of line that earns genuine laughter from comedy-savvy audiences because it's not the obvious comparison. Highly quotable. Chandler at his most incisive, holding Ross accountable with a perfectly constructed one-liner.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I can't see through the door!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's kind of what doors do.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'And the inventor of the door rests happily in his grave.'
jokes.setup: Ross is watching through the peephole to see if Rachel kisses Mark; the door closes and he can't see anything
jokes.punchline: Chandler offers a deadpan eulogy for the door's inventor — implicitly thanking him for blocking Ross's surveillance
jokes.explanation: A beautifully written one-liner. The absurdist image of praising a long-dead door inventor for his unknowing contribution to blocking Ross's jealousy is original and perfectly economical. 'Rests happily in his grave' is a specific, poetic phrase that elevates the joke beyond a simple comment. This is the kind of line that gets quoted. Strong craft across all dimensions.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica has numbered her coffee mugs. They're numbered one through twelve.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Numbered? Why would she number them?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Because she says each mug holds a different amount of coffee based on the ceramic density and the glaze thickness, so she needs to know which one to use depending on what type of coffee she's making.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's insane.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's not insane, it's efficient! Mug number seven is for cappuccino, mug number three is for americano, and mug number eleven is for when I'm really tired and need the extra half-ounce of coffee that the wider rim provides.

jokes.text: Ross's increasingly frantic attempts to get across the hall to stop whatever is happening — 'I need juice. People need juice.'
jokes.setup: Ross is convinced he needs to go interrupt Rachel and Mark; Chandler physically holds him back
jokes.punchline: Ross's justification devolves into the increasingly desperate 'I need juice. People need juice. Juice.' — as if universal human need for juice is sufficient reason to barge in
jokes.explanation: The desperation escalation of 'I need juice' → 'People need juice' → 'Juice' is a strong comedic deconstruction. By the end, Ross has reduced his argument to a single noun, which is perfect. Combined with Chandler physically restraining him and Ross calling him 'surprisingly strong,' this whole sequence is quality physical-plus-verbal comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm using you to get back at Ross.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Oh, okay! Yeah, that's fine. Whatever you need.

jokes.text: Chandler: '...unless you're thinking about subletting my peephole, you are gonna have to get used to the fact that the relationship is over.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is delivering a serious speech to Ross about moving on from Rachel
jokes.punchline: He throws in 'unless you're thinking about subletting my peephole' — a real-estate joke that riffs on both their New York apartment context and the peephole surveillance that's been happening
jokes.explanation: Good callback joke embedded in an emotional scene. 'Subletting my peephole' is a New York-specific real-estate joke combined with the running visual of Ross at the door. It lightens the serious speech while remaining tonally appropriate. Chandler's comedy in serious moments is a series hallmark.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Fine! I'll just go home and do it myself then!

jokes.text: Ross (near tears, after the emotional scene): 'Why do all your coffee mugs have numbers on the bottom?' / Chandler: 'Oh, that's so Monica can keep track. That way, if one of them is missing, she can be like, Where's number 27?'
jokes.setup: The emotional scene between Ross and Chandler winds down; Ross suddenly notices something odd about the mugs
jokes.punchline: The explanation reveals Monica has a numbered inventory system for coffee mugs — a perfect expression of her obsessive, controlling personality
jokes.explanation: A tonal relief valve joke after the emotional Ross-Chandler scene. It also scores well on character integration: the numbered mug inventory is entirely consistent with Monica's established obsessive-compulsive tendencies. The specificity of 'Where's number 27?' makes it funnier than a vague reference to her neatness.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Where are we?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, we're either in a hospital, or this is a really depressing Pottery Barn.

jokes.text: Mark: 'Fair, shmair. You know? Look, you wanna get back at Ross, I am here for you. I say we get back at him right here on this couch.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has just told Mark she can't date him because she's only doing it to get back at Ross, not because she genuinely likes him
jokes.punchline: Mark cheerfully says 'fair, shmair' and suggests they go ahead and get back at Ross on the couch anyway — volunteering to be used with complete enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Mark's shameless willingness to be used as a pawn against Ross is funny because it's completely transparent and self-aware. 'Fair, shmair' is a nice character-specific phrase. The humor is in his complete lack of self-respect being played as confident pragmatism.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: What? Monica's not attracted to me? But I'm like... I'm like a young Marlon Brando!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You're like a young Shelley Winters.

jokes.text: Mark: 'I can just go home and get back at him by myself.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has rejected Mark's offer to make out on the couch; he accepts gracefully
jokes.punchline: He casually mentions he'll 'get back at Ross by himself' — implying he'll go home and... use his imagination about Rachel — delivered with complete composure
jokes.explanation: This is a sharp, dark, economical joke that pushes the Friends format slightly. The implication is clear but not explicitly stated, which is the right level of edginess for the show. The casual, composed delivery makes it funnier than a more obvious version would be. 'By myself' does all the work in two words. Good economy and originality — this is a slightly bolder joke than Friends typically attempts.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know what? I think it's great that you're so confident even after being rejected.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: Well, I know I'm a catch. I mean, look at me. I'm charming, I'm successful, I'm handsome...

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: The rejection just means she has terrible taste.

jokes.text: Pete's speech to a hospital crowd gets interrupted — Monica says 'Where are we?' and Pete deadpans 'Well, with all these doctors and nurses, I'm gonna say, Midget Rodeo.'
jokes.setup: Monica asks where they are (genuinely unsure); Pete is about to give a speech to medical professionals
jokes.punchline: 'Midget Rodeo' — Pete offers a completely absurd wrong answer when the obvious answer (a hospital) is staring them in the face
jokes.explanation: 'Midget Rodeo' is a left-field absurdist choice that earns its laugh through specificity — it's not just 'a rodeo' or 'a circus,' it's 'Midget Rodeo,' which is funnier for being more specific and more inexplicable. Pete's delivery of this with complete confidence while surrounded by obvious medical professionals is the right framing.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's not a woman's shirt!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, but I'm just saying, if a woman came out of the bathroom and she was wearing that shirt, I'd still recognize her.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm going to the gym every day. I'm going to get bigger. I'm going to get really, really big.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's great, sweetie. In the meantime, why don't you just... take it off?

jokes.text: Monica: 'I so want to be attracted to you.' Pete: 'But you're not. Okay. Good.'
jokes.setup: Monica is struggling to let Pete down gently by explaining she wants to feel attraction but doesn't
jokes.punchline: Pete responds with 'But you're not. Okay. Good.' — a rapid, matter-of-fact acceptance that undercuts the emotional weight of the confession
jokes.explanation: The rapid-fire 'But you're not. Okay. Good.' is funny because it's so business-like about a painful admission. Pete immediately moves on, which establishes him as confident and unfazed in a way that's charming and comedic simultaneously. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more out of this conversation?

jokes.text: Pete: 'I know I'm no Jon Bon Jovi. Or someone you find attractive.'
jokes.setup: Pete is explaining why Monica might come around to being attracted to him despite her current feelings
jokes.punchline: He compares himself to Jon Bon Jovi and then immediately clarifies — or someone she actually finds attractive — implying Jon Bon Jovi himself might be an aspirational standard Pete can't reach either
jokes.explanation: The self-deprecating qualification — 'or someone you find attractive' — is a nice additional beat. It's not clear if he's saying Bon Jovi IS attractive or if he's admitting he falls below even that bar. The ambiguity adds a layer. Decent joke, well delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. So you're saying that Kate thinks she's better than Sliced Bread?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I didn't know Sliced Bread was an actress.

jokes.text: Monica: 'You seem awfully confident for a guy I just told I wasn't attracted to.' Pete: 'Yeah, stupidly charming, isn't it?'
jokes.setup: Pete continues to be upbeat and persistent despite Monica's rejection
jokes.punchline: Monica calls out his weird confidence; Pete agrees it's 'stupidly charming' — a self-aware admission that his confidence is its own kind of absurdity
jokes.explanation: 'Stupidly charming, isn't it?' is a genuinely good line — Pete acknowledges the absurdity of his confidence while simultaneously demonstrating it. It's self-aware without being meta in a way that breaks character. The structure of calling your own behavior 'stupidly charming' while clearly believing it works is well constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I hate how she's always trying to upstage me on set. I hate how she never learns her lines. I hate how she smells like a combination of tuna fish and regret.

jokes.text: Ross entering his apartment in tiny T-shirt and immediately acting like it's a showdown: 'I don't think this town is big enough for the both of us to relax in.'
jokes.setup: Ross returns home in the tiny T-shirt; Chandler is sitting in their apartment relaxing
jokes.punchline: Ross does a full Western-movie standoff routine — 'I don't think this town is big enough for the both of us to relax in' — while visually ridiculous in his tiny shirt
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels simultaneously: the Western movie parody is well-constructed ('this town isn't big enough for the both of us' adapted to 'relax in'), AND it's physically hilarious because Ross is playing this macho role in a tiny, tight shirt. The combination of the visual callback and the comedic dialogue is strong. Rewatch bonus because the shirt gag keeps delivering.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I think someone has a crush on you.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: On me? Really?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, no. I mean you have a crush on someone.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Draw.'
jokes.setup: Ross has just delivered a Western movie ultimatum
jokes.punchline: Chandler plays along with a single word: 'Draw.' — committing to the bit with perfect economy
jokes.explanation: One word, perfectly timed. 'Draw' is the ideal response to Ross's setup — it fully commits to the Western bit without over-explaining it. Economy is a 10: there is literally nothing more efficient possible. Good callback to the Western theme.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You're like a kid in a candy store.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What candy store? Where?

jokes.text: Ross: 'I wasn't doing anything.' [flat denial after the Western standoff]
jokes.setup: Chandler says 'Draw'; Ross is in full Western mode
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately drops the bit and flatly denies having done anything — as if none of the preceding nonsense happened
jokes.explanation: The punctuation on the Western bit. Ross's complete abandonment of the persona with 'I wasn't doing anything' is a nice button. Works as a three-part comedy beat: setup (Ross's Western speech), escalation (Chandler's 'Draw'), deflation (Ross's denial). The sequence as a whole is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Your scene was really great. You were really... great.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: And you know what? I believed you. I believed that you were a person.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Uh-oh. What did she do now?' and then: 'Just because she went to Yale Drama, she thinks she's like the greatest actress since sliced bread.' Chandler: 'Ah, Sliced Bread. A wonderful Lady Macbeth.'
jokes.setup: Joey is complaining about Kate; he mixes up the idiom 'greatest thing since sliced bread' by using it as if sliced bread itself is an actress
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately plays along, treating 'Sliced Bread' as an actress famous for her Lady Macbeth — validating Joey's mistake as if it were intentional
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly constructed joke built on Joey's malapropism. Joey accidentally creates a nonsense idiom by misapplying 'greatest thing since sliced bread' — and Chandler's response elevates it by treating 'Sliced Bread' as a legitimate historical actress with a notable stage credit. 'A wonderful Lady Macbeth' is the perfect specific detail. High character integration: only Joey makes this error, and only Chandler responds this way. This is one of the episode's best jokes — fast, layered, and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, so his name is Peter Parker, right? But he's Spider-Man. So why isn't he Peter Spider?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Because that's not how it works.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, no, I'm serious! If Clark Kent is Superman, then Peter Parker should be Spider-Man... I mean, Peter Spider. What if there was a guy named Phil? He'd be Phil Spider!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: And he'd be a regular guy.

jokes.text: Joey describes hating Kate with 'Oh, I'm so talented, and oh, I'm so pretty, and oh, I smell so good'
jokes.setup: Joey is venting about Kate's arrogance
jokes.punchline: His complaints escalate to include that she 'smells so good' — betraying that he's attracted to her while pretending to hate her
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'talented' and 'pretty' (legitimate complaints) to 'smells so good' is the tell — Joey has crossed from criticism into description of attraction. It's a neat, economical piece of character revelation disguised as a rant.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. So we have Superman, Batman, Iron Man... there's gotta be a Gold Man.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: There is no Gold Man, Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, there should be!

jokes.text: Chandler: 'I think somebody has a crush on somebody.' / Joey: 'Hey, Chandler, can we please try and stay focused on my problem here? I'm talking about you, you big, big freak.'
jokes.setup: Chandler suggests Joey has a crush on Kate based on the intensity of his hatred for her
jokes.punchline: Joey dismisses Chandler's theory, tells him to focus on Joey's 'problem' — and then immediately calls Chandler a 'big, big freak' for suggesting it, which is itself evidence of the exact displacement Chandler described
jokes.explanation: A good character moment — Joey's angry denial of having a crush proves the crush theory. The 'you big, big freak' insult is characteristically Joey. The joke is in the dramatic irony of Joey's blindness to his own feelings.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Work went great today.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I mean, I did trip over my own feet in front of my boss and spilled coffee all over myself, but other than that, great.

jokes.text: Chandler pointing out that Joey 'would be pulling her pigtails and pushing her down' if they were in a schoolyard — and Joey's 'Oh, yeah? Then how come I keep thinking about her in all these sexual scenarios and stuff, huh?'
jokes.setup: Chandler explains that Joey's obsessive hatred of Kate is classic crush behavior
jokes.punchline: Joey tries to refute the crush theory with evidence — then immediately provides MORE evidence of the crush by mentioning he thinks about her in 'sexual scenarios'
jokes.explanation: An excellently structured joke. Joey begins a sentence designed to disprove Chandler's crush theory and ends it by completely confirming it. The self-own is total and immediate. 'In all these sexual scenarios and stuff' is perfectly Joey — the vagueness of 'and stuff' and the plural 'scenarios' implying there are many. This is a great character comedy moment that earns its impact score.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What about things that are already gold? Can he gold them?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, they're already gold. His job is done.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Oh, yeah? Then how come I keep thinking about her in all these sexual scenarios and stuff, huh?'
jokes.setup: Joey denies having a crush on Kate, insisting it's just hate
jokes.punchline: He attempts to prove he has no crush by... admitting to constant sexual fantasies about her, apparently not seeing the contradiction
jokes.explanation: Excellent Joey joke. His complete failure to see that sexual fantasies confirm rather than deny attraction is precisely the kind of oblivious self-contradiction Joey commits constantly. 'In all these sexual scenarios and stuff' is wonderfully Joey in phrasing — casual and vague. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm gonna do it. I'm gonna do the whole thing.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, this is gonna be good.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: All right, here we go.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, because nothing says 'cool gunslinger' like a guy who can't fit into his pants.

jokes.text: Joey saying 'Nothing' during the play — and the director responds 'You guys make me fly.' Joey later corrects 'fly' to 'high'
jokes.setup: Joey and Kate are running their emotional scene; at the climactic 'Nothing' beat, the director responds with artistic rapture
jokes.punchline: The director says 'You guys make me fly' — an ecstatic malapropism; Joey corrects it to 'high.' The implication is the director is either stoned or just mangling his own emotion
jokes.explanation: A gentle joke at the pretentious director's expense. 'You guys make me fly' is either a malapropism, an affectation, or evidence of drug use — all three possibilities are funny. Joey's flat 'High' correction is a good deadpan reaction beat. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Director describing the rehearsal as 'better' / 'definitely an improvement' — visibly struggling
jokes.setup: After the intense run-through, the director gives feedback
jokes.punchline: He settles on 'definitely an improvement' — the weakest possible praise that still technically qualifies as praise — implying the rehearsal was mediocre but he's being polite
jokes.explanation: A mild joke built on damning with faint praise. Functional but unremarkable — the humor is in the director's obvious struggle to say something positive. Below average for this episode.

jokes.text: Kate leaving without her shoes — 'I'm probably gonna need those, huh?'
jokes.setup: Joey calls after Kate that she's forgotten her shoes; Kate is so flustered (presumably by Joey) that she walked out without noticing
jokes.punchline: Kate's embarrassed admission — 'I'm probably gonna need those, huh?' — suggests she was distracted enough to forget basic footwear, confirming Joey's theory about her feelings
jokes.explanation: A nice visual comedy beat that confirms what the audience already suspects — Kate has feelings for Joey too. The embarrassed understatement of 'I'm probably gonna need those, huh?' is charming. Rewatch bonus because it's a clear 'confirmation' moment.

jokes.text: Ross and Chandler debating why it's not 'Spiderman' like Goldman or Silverman — 'It's not his last name. It's not like Phil Spiderman.'
jokes.setup: Ross (or Chandler) wonders why Spider-Man isn't written as one word like surnames (Goldman, Silverman)
jokes.punchline: The explanation is that Spider-Man isn't Phil Spiderman — he's a spider-man, a man who is also a spider, not a man whose family name is Spiderman
jokes.explanation: A surprisingly sharp bit of pop-culture linguistic analysis. 'Phil Spiderman' is a great specific name choice that makes the absurdist alternative funny and concrete. This is the kind of observational riff that male characters in sitcoms do well, and it works here because the logic is internally consistent and the delivery is deadpan.

jokes.text: Ross/Chandler: 'He's a spider... man.' / 'You know, like Goldman is a last name. But there's no gold man.' / 'Oh, okay. There should be a Gold Man.'
jokes.setup: The Spider-Man naming logic has established that compound superhero names describe what the hero IS, not their surname
jokes.punchline: Joey responds to the absence of a gold man by declaring 'there should be a Gold Man' — treating the lack of a literal gold person as a gap in the universe that should be filled
jokes.explanation: Joey's 'There should be a Gold Man' is the perfect capper to the Spider-Man riff. It extends the bit naturally and ends it on an absurdist but perfectly Joey note — he's not confused, he's genuinely optimistic about the possibility of a Gold Man existing. Great character integration.

jokes.text: Rachel opening Ross's box of her stuff and finding the tiny T-shirt — the camera holds on her emotional reaction
jokes.setup: Monica mentions Ross dropped off a box of Rachel's stuff; Rachel expects it to be junk ('probably just shampoo') and is about to throw it away
jokes.punchline: She finds the tiny T-shirt — the one Ross made such a scene over — and has a visible emotional reaction, revealing she cares more than she admitted
jokes.explanation: This is technically more of a dramatic beat than pure comedy, but it earns a place here as a reaction beat with comedic resonance — the T-shirt that was the subject of a petty, ridiculous argument is revealed to have genuine emotional weight. The audience laughs with recognition and a touch of sadness. It's a well-crafted payoff to the T-shirt subplot that elevates what could have been pure slapstick into something more resonant. 'Hmm. No. Nothing.' as Rachel's denial is its own small joke.

jokes.text: 'What kind of powers would Gold Man have?' / 'He would turn things to gold.' / 'What about things that are already gold?' / 'Ah. His work is done.'
jokes.setup: Joey's 'There should be a Gold Man' is taken seriously as a superhero concept; the group now develops Gold Man's powers
jokes.punchline: When asked about things already gold, the answer is 'his work is done' — Gold Man has no jurisdiction over pre-existing gold, therefore his utility is hilariously limited
jokes.explanation: An excellent comedic escalation of the Gold Man concept. The logical question — what about things already gold? — and the perfectly confident answer — 'his work is done' — is a brilliantly absurdist closing joke. The phrase 'his work is done' implies Gold Man has completed some cosmic task just by existing, which is both hilarious and weirdly poetic. High quotability. Great way to close the episode on a lighter note after the emotional Rachel beat.
